label: Strategies
labelTooltip: Sensory strategies recommended for this child's sensory profile

children.text: Provide regular, scheduled sensory breaks throughout the day to help the CYP manage heightened internal signals
Use visual supports such as body maps or emotion scales to help the CYP identify and label internal body signals
Offer a calm, low-stimulation area where the CYP can go when feeling overwhelmed by internal sensations
Teach and practise regulation strategies such as deep breathing, progressive muscle relaxation, or grounding techniques
Provide predictable routines around eating, drinking, and toileting to reduce anxiety about internal sensations
Use social stories to help the CYP understand and manage their responses to internal signals such as hunger, pain, or temperature changes
Work with the CYP to create a personalised regulation toolkit that includes preferred calming strategies
Allow flexible access to water, snacks, and toilet facilities to reduce distress from heightened awareness of internal needs
Implement scheduled prompts for toileting, eating, and drinking rather than relying on the CYP to recognise their own needs
Use visual timetables or timers as prompts for regular hydration and meal breaks
Teach the CYP to use a body check-in routine at regular intervals to notice internal sensations
Use the Zones of Regulation or similar programme to develop emotional awareness and link feelings to body signals
Monitor the CYP during physical activity and set boundaries to prevent over-exertion as they may not feel fatigue
Provide explicit teaching about what different internal signals feel like using concrete examples and visuals
Use co-regulation strategies such as modelling your own awareness of internal states aloud
Use structured interoception activities such as mindful body scans to build awareness of internal signals
Teach the CYP to discriminate between different internal signals using visual supports and concrete language
Provide support to link internal body signals to actions, e.g. 'When your tummy growls, that means you are hungry'
Use resources from Kelly Mahler's interoception curriculum to develop body-signal awareness
Partner with parents/carers to reinforce interoception awareness at home using consistent language and strategies
Allow for flexible seating and positioning options so the CYP can find comfortable positions
Provide activities that offer gentle, graded proprioceptive input such as yoga or stretching
Offer adapted tools for fine motor tasks such as thicker pencils or pencil grips to reduce proprioceptive demand
Allow the CYP to stand or move during tasks if sitting is uncomfortable
Avoid forcing the CYP into positions or movements that cause distress
Provide regular heavy work activities such as carrying books, pushing, pulling, or wall press-ups
Use weighted lap pads, weighted blankets, or compression clothing to provide additional proprioceptive input
Incorporate movement breaks with resistive activities into the daily routine
Offer chewy items or crunchy snacks as an oral proprioceptive input strategy
Use a wobble cushion, therapy ball, or move-n-sit cushion for seating to increase proprioceptive feedback
Encourage the CYP to help with physical classroom tasks such as stacking chairs or moving equipment
Provide planned opportunities for deep pressure activities throughout the day
Allow access to fidget tools, resistance bands on chair legs, or textured items
Schedule regular movement breaks involving pushing, pulling, jumping, or climbing
Provide a body sock, lycra tunnel, or den space for the CYP to access calming deep pressure
Offer chew toys or chewable necklaces as a safe alternative to chewing on clothing or objects
Use firm touch or deep pressure when interacting with the CYP rather than light touch
Allow the CYP to wrap themselves in blankets or use a weighted blanket during calm times
Offer choices during PE and physical activities so the CYP can participate at a level that feels safe
Provide advance warning of any activities involving movement, changes of direction, or heights
Allow the CYP to keep their feet on the ground during activities where possible
Use graded exposure to help the CYP gradually build tolerance to movement activities
Position the CYP near the edge of group activities so they are less affected by others' movement
Avoid spinning or swinging activities unless the CYP chooses to participate
Provide stability aids such as a stable chair (not a swivel chair) and ensure feet can touch the floor
Provide regular opportunities for controlled movement activities such as rocking, swinging, or bouncing
Use a wobble cushion, rocking chair, or therapy ball for seating to provide vestibular input
Build movement breaks into the daily routine to meet the CYP's need for vestibular stimulation
Incorporate spinning, rolling, and direction-change activities into PE and break times
Teach the CYP to recognise when they need movement and provide appropriate outlets
Allow the CYP to stand or move while working if remaining still is difficult
Schedule regular movement breaks with spinning, swinging, or bouncing activities
Provide safe climbing opportunities during break times
Use a sit-and-spin, swing, or rocking horse at designated times
Allow the CYP to run errands that involve walking or moving around the school
Incorporate rhythmic movement such as marching, skipping, or dancing into transitions
Provide a fidget tool or allow rocking during seated activities to safely meet vestibular needs
Ensure the CYP has safe spaces for high-energy movement to reduce risk of injury
Position the CYP at the end of a line or on the edge of a group to reduce unexpected touch
Use firm, predictable touch rather than light or unexpected touch
Give advance warning before any physical contact, including during activities like PE or art
Allow the CYP to remove clothing labels, wear seamless socks, or choose clothing that feels comfortable
Offer alternatives to messy play activities or provide tools such as paintbrushes or gloves
Provide the CYP with their own clearly defined space using a mat, tape, or desk divider
Use a 'hands-up' approach when gaining the CYP's attention rather than tapping their shoulder
Provide opportunities for messy play, water play, and tactile exploration
Use vibrating pens or textured grips to increase tactile feedback during writing
Offer clothing with a tighter fit or compression garments if preferred by the CYP
Provide tactile prompts for self-care routines, such as visual reminders to check if face or hands are clean
Include tactile elements in learning activities, such as textured letters, sand trays, or modelling clay
Provide a box of tactile items (koosh balls, putty, textured fabrics) for the CYP to access during lessons
Teach the CYP about personal space and boundaries using social stories and role play
Offer fidget tools that provide tactile input such as tangles, putty, or textured fidgets
Provide regular opportunities for deep pressure activities as an alternative to touching others
Include sensory exploration activities in the curriculum, such as sensory bins or feely bags
Allow barefoot activities in safe environments if the CYP prefers this
Reduce visual clutter in the classroom — use neutral colours, minimal displays, and organised storage
Seat the CYP away from windows and bright lights, or allow them to wear a cap or sunglasses indoors
Use pastel or cream-coloured paper instead of white to reduce glare
Provide advance warning of any changes to the classroom layout
Use blinds or curtains to control natural light and reduce flickering
Position the CYP's desk to minimise distracting visual stimuli from other pupils' movement
Allow the CYP to use a reading window or line guide to reduce visual overload when reading
Offer visual breaks — allow the CYP to look away from the board or close their eyes briefly
Use high-contrast materials and bold, clear fonts for written work
Highlight key information using colour coding or bold text
Allow the CYP to sit closer to the board or screen
Use enlarged text and images where necessary
Provide additional verbal description alongside visual materials
Use tactile or multi-sensory approaches to supplement visual learning tasks
Provide hand-over-hand guidance for tasks requiring hand-eye coordination
Provide access to light-up toys, lava lamps, or fibre-optic lights at designated times
Allow access to visually stimulating fidget tools such as glitter jars or liquid motion timers
Redirect visual seeking behaviour towards functional visual tasks or activities
Use visual schedules and colour-coded systems to channel the CYP's visual interest productively
Provide a visual sensory box with items like kaleidoscopes, spinning tops, or reflective materials
Seat the CYP where they can observe the room without needing to turn around frequently
Provide ear defenders or noise-cancelling headphones for use in noisy environments
Give advance warning of any expected loud noises such as fire alarms, bells, or assemblies
Allow the CYP to leave noisy environments or arrive/leave slightly early to avoid busy transition times
Seat the CYP away from sources of background noise such as fans, open windows, or doorways
Reduce unnecessary noise in the classroom by using soft furnishings, tennis balls on chair legs, or felt pads
Provide a quiet, low-stimulation space for the CYP to retreat to when overwhelmed
Use visual cues and instructions alongside verbal communication to reduce auditory demand
Use the CYP's name before giving instructions to gain their attention
Pair verbal instructions with visual supports to ensure understanding
Check understanding by asking the CYP to repeat back instructions
Allow the CYP to sit close to the speaker during input to improve auditory access
Provide auditory enrichment activities such as music or sound-based games to promote engagement
Provide headphones with music during independent work if this supports focus
Offer access to musical instruments or sound-making toys at appropriate times
Allow the CYP to hum or make quiet sounds if this helps self-regulation, where possible
Incorporate rhythm and music into learning activities
Redirect disruptive noise-making into appropriate channels such as drumming on a pad or using a fidget with sound
Use a 'noise meter' visual to help the CYP self-monitor their volume level
Provide a designated space where louder activities are acceptable, such as a music corner
Avoid placing pressure on the CYP to try new foods — use a gradual exposure approach
Allow the CYP to bring preferred foods from home for mealtimes and snacks
Provide a calm, low-stimulation environment for eating to reduce anxiety around mealtimes
Work with parents/carers and consider referral to a feeding specialist if the limited diet is impacting health
Use food exploration activities (touching, smelling, looking) before expecting the CYP to taste new foods
Respect the CYP's food preferences and avoid using food as a reward or punishment
Supervise the CYP closely to prevent mouthing or eating non-food items (pica risk)
Provide safe oral motor tools such as chew tubes or chewable jewellery as alternatives
Monitor food intake and provide prompts for eating and drinking at regular intervals
Present food in an appealing way and offer varied textures and flavours to support engagement with eating
Provide crunchy, chewy, or strong-flavoured snacks at planned break times
Offer safe chewing alternatives such as chew necklaces, chew tubes, or crunchy raw vegetables
Ensure non-food items are kept out of reach and redirect mouthing to safe alternatives
Plan oral sensory activities such as blowing bubbles, using whistles, or drinking through straws
Work with the CYP and their family to establish a balanced approach to food seeking
Teach the CYP about appropriate portion sizes using visual supports
Avoid using strong-scented cleaning products, air fresheners, or perfumes in the CYP's environment
Seat the CYP away from potential odour sources such as kitchens, toilets, or bins
Allow the CYP to use a preferred scent on a handkerchief or wristband to mask unpleasant smells
Provide a low-odour, well-ventilated eating environment for mealtimes
Give advance warning if an activity will involve strong smells, such as cooking or science experiments
Implement a structured personal hygiene routine with visual prompts and reminders
Monitor toileting and provide appropriate support and prompts
Use strong or distinctive scents in learning activities to enhance engagement
Address any smearing behaviour with medical and sensory support — consider underlying sensory need
Sensitively support the CYP with personal hygiene while maintaining their dignity
Provide a scent kit with a range of safe, pleasant scents for the CYP to access at agreed times
Incorporate scented materials into learning activities, such as scented markers or scratch-and-sniff resources
Redirect inappropriate smelling behaviour to accepted alternatives
Use aromatherapy or scented oils in a calm area to provide a safe outlet for olfactory seeking
